meta.name: Posture IQ
meta.disclaimer: This assessment provides advisory guidance to support architecture and governance decisions. It is not a legal opinion. Specific interpretations of GDPR, NIS2, DORA, the EU AI Act, EUCS and UK data protection law should be confirmed with qualified counsel and your competent supervisory authority.

regulations.desc: Lawful processing, international transfers (Ch. V), processor obligations, security of processing.

regulations.desc: Post-Brexit UK regime; international transfers via IDTA / UK Addendum; ICO oversight.

regulations.name: NIS2
regulations.desc: Essential/important entity duties, supply-chain security, governance accountability, incident reporting.

regulations.name: DORA
regulations.desc: ICT risk management, third-party risk, register of information, critical function outsourcing, concentration risk.

regulations.name: EU AI Act
regulations.desc: Data governance for high-risk AI (Art. 10), record-keeping, human oversight, GPAI obligations.

regulations.name: EUCS

regulations.desc: Assurance levels (Basic/Substantial/High) and sovereignty-related requirements for cloud services.

regulations.name: EU Data Act
regulations.full: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 on harmonised rules on fair access to and use of data
regulations.tag: EU · cloud switching & non-personal data access
regulations.desc: Cloud switching and portability obligations for data-processing services; safeguards against unlawful third-country access to non-personal data held in the EU. Applies from 12 September 2025; switching provisions phased.

regulations.name: UK Op Res
regulations.full: FCA PS21/3; PRA SS2/21 — Operational Resilience
regulations.desc: Impact tolerances for important business services, mapping, scenario testing, self-assessment and outsourcing / third-party risk expectations.

regulations.name: UK CTP
regulations.full: Financial Services and Markets Act 2023, Part 9; FCA PS24/16; PRA PS16/24
regulations.desc: HM Treasury designations of Critical Third Parties to the UK financial sector; joint FCA / PRA / BoE oversight; six Fundamental Rules.

regulations.name: UK AI approach
regulations.full: ICO Guidance on AI and data protection; FCA AI update; PRA/BoE SS1/23 (Model risk management for AI/ML)
regulations.desc: UK operates a principles-based, regulator-led approach to AI rather than a UK equivalent of the EU AI Act. ICO guidance on AI and data protection, FCA supervisory expectations for AI in regulated activities, and PRA/BoE SS1/23 on model risk management for AI/ML apply. Track further UK regulatory evolution.

PRA / Bank of England SS1/23 — Model risk

sections.title: Regulatory scope & entity classification
sections.desc: Establishes which obligations bite. NIS2 and DORA impose sharply different duties depending on how your entity is classified.

sections.title: Data asset inventory & classification
sections.desc: You cannot protect residency for data you have not classified. This maps sensitive categories to volume and criticality.

sections.title: Data location & residency
sections.desc: Where each category of data is stored and processed today, across cloud regions, SaaS and on-premises estate.

sections.title: International transfers & transfer mechanisms
sections.desc: Post-Schrems II, any flow of personal data outside the EEA/UK needs a valid mechanism and a transfer impact assessment.

sections.title: Third-party processors & ICT supply chain

sections.desc: Where backups live, how data is encrypted, and whether resilience arrangements themselves create residency exposure.

sections.title: Governance, contracts & audit rights
sections.desc: Contractual audit rights, subprocessor control, register of information and accountable ownership.

dynamicProbes.name: The Residency Illusion Anomaly
dynamicProbes.clientAssertion: We host all production workloads in AWS Frankfurt / Azure Dublin, so GDPR Chapter V and DORA residency are fully satisfied.
dynamicProbes.statutoryConflict: Physical localization in Frankfurt or Dublin satisfies the territorial criterion, but leaves extraterritorial reach unmitigated. Under the US CLOUD Act (18 U.S.C. § 2713) and FISA §702, US law enforcement can issue lawful access orders directly to the US parent entity. Absent Hold-Your-Own-Key (HYOK) with client-held HSMs, the cloud provider can be compelled to decrypt data without client notice, directly conflicting with GDPR Art. 48 and EU Data Act Art. 32.
dynamicProbes.interrogationScript: Physical localization in Frankfurt satisfies half the equation, but leaves legal reach completely unmitigated. Under the US CLOUD Act, your contract with a US-headquartered parent entity means US courts have legal reach over the data, regardless of physical location. If a lawful access order is served, can you technically prevent the provider from decrypting data? Who on your executive risk committee has formally approved this residual legal exposure?

dynamicProbes.name: The Enterprise SaaS Administrative Blindspot
dynamicProbes.clientAssertion: Microsoft 365, Salesforce, and ServiceNow are standard enterprise SaaS tools covered by our corporate SOC 2 and ISO 27001 certifications.
dynamicProbes.statutoryConflict: Enterprise SaaS represents the largest unmapped data leakage channel in modern enterprises. Multi-tenant SaaS environments routinely grant global SREs and support engineers follow-the-sun privileged access to diagnose incidents. Tenant data is encrypted with vendor-managed keys, violating DORA Art. 28 and NIS2 Art. 21 supply chain obligations.
dynamicProbes.interrogationScript: Enterprise SaaS represents the single largest unmapped data leakage channel in modern enterprises. While customer data sits in regional datacenters, vendor support engineers operating out of follow-the-sun global centers possess privileged access to diagnose incidents. Have you implemented Customer Lockbox to mandate explicit approval for every vendor session, and deployed tenant-held cache keys (such as M365 Customer Key or Salesforce Shield) to enforce cryptographic opacity?

dynamicProbes.name: The DORA & APRA Concentration Cliff (The Exit Strategy Myth)
dynamicProbes.clientAssertion: Our primary cloud provider has four Availability Zones and a 99.99% SLA. Our exit plan is documented in our annual Disaster Recovery handbook.
dynamicProbes.statutoryConflict: DORA Art. 28(8), UK CTP (FSMA 2023 Part 9), and APRA CPS 230 explicitly mandate tested, feasible exit strategies from Critical ICT Third-Party Providers (CTPPs). A Disaster Recovery plan within the same hyperscaler does not qualify as an exit strategy. If the provider suffers a systemic outage, sanctions, or contractual dispute, moving proprietary PaaS services takes 18–24+ months without containerized portability.
dynamicProbes.interrogationScript: Regulators distinguish sharply between high availability and vendor exitability. DORA and APRA require an auditable playbook to migrate critical functions away from a concentrated provider without operational disruption. When was the last time you simulated an actual technical cutover of a core business service to an alternative provider or private cloud enclave? If your primary provider experienced a systemic lockout, what is your verified cutover timeline?

dynamicProbes.name: Unregulated AI Training Data Drift
dynamicProbes.badge: EU AI Act Art. 10 Statutory Exposure
dynamicProbes.clientAssertion: Our AI models were trained internally on enterprise data, and we access external LLMs via enterprise APIs with zero-retention contractual clauses.
dynamicProbes.statutoryConflict: EU AI Act Art. 10 imposes strict governance mandates on high-risk AI data provenance, bias mitigation, and training validation. Processing European customer data through out-of-region compute instances or fine-tuning models without auditable training lineage can trigger penalties of up to €15M or 3% of worldwide turnover under Art. 99(4).
dynamicProbes.interrogationScript: The EU AI Act and GDPR treat AI inference and fine-tuning as restricted data processing. If prompt tokens or fine-tuning datasets traverse out-of-EEA compute nodes, you face compounding penalties under both GDPR Chapter V and AI Act Art. 10. Do you possess an immutable provenance register verifying exactly which training epochs touched customer data, and are your GenAI workloads confined to certified EU sovereign AI fabrics?

dynamicProbes.name: The Remote Management Telemetry Backdoor
dynamicProbes.clientAssertion: Our critical core runs on-premises in our own private data center; therefore, we have zero foreign access exposure.
dynamicProbes.statutoryConflict: Modern enterprise server management controllers (Dell iDRAC, HPE iLO), storage arrays, and network firewalls frequently maintain active telemetry and remote diagnostic tunnels (call-home) connected to foreign vendor support clouds. This creates an unmonitored management plane backdoor bypassing perimeter controls under NIS2 Art. 21.
dynamicProbes.interrogationScript: While physical servers sit inside your perimeter, the management plane often connects outbound to foreign vendor telemetry centers. Are your out-of-band management controllers strictly air-gapped on isolated VLANs with all phone-home diagnostic telemetry blocked? Has the hardware bill of materials been audited against clean supply chain standards (such as NDAA Section 889)?

dynamicProbes.name: The Cloud-Native KMS Lock-In (The BYOK Illusion)
dynamicProbes.clientAssertion: We use AWS KMS and Azure Key Vault with our own Customer Managed Keys (CMK), so the cloud provider cannot decrypt our data.
dynamicProbes.statutoryConflict: A cloud-native CMK is still hosted inside the cloud provider's hardware security modules (HSMs). The provider's hypervisor executes cryptographic operations in plaintext in volatile RAM. Under FISA §702 or CLOUD Act direct subpoenas, the provider can be compelled to decrypt workloads in memory without client involvement, failing EDPB Schrems II supplementary measure requirements.
dynamicProbes.interrogationScript: Cloud-managed keys (CMK) protect against external hackers, but provide zero legal protection against the cloud provider itself. Under cloud-native KMS, the provider controls the hypervisor and the HSM where your key is instantiated. If the provider is compelled under a lawful access warrant, they possess the technical ability to decrypt your workloads in volatile RAM. True technical defensibility requires Hold-Your-Own-Key (HYOK)—where the root of trust resides in external HSMs under your exclusive physical control.

questions.text: Under NIS2, how is your entity classified?
questions.help: NIS2 splits organisations into 'essential' and 'important' entities, each with different supervisory and penalty regimes. Classification usually follows sector and size.

options.label: Essential entity (e.g. energy, transport, banking, health, digital infrastructure, ICT service management)

findings.title: Essential-entity supervisory regime applies
findings.detail: As an essential entity you are subject to proactive (ex-ante) supervision, on-site inspections and the highest tier of administrative fines (up to €10m or 2% of global turnover).
findings.remedy: Confirm classification with your national competent authority and register accordingly.
steps: Confirm classification against the national NIS2 transposition
Register with the competent authority within the national deadline
Map essential-entity obligations to an accountable executive owner

options.label: Important entity (e.g. manufacturing, postal, waste, chemicals, food, digital providers)

findings.title: Important-entity duties apply
findings.detail: Important entities face ex-post supervision but the same core security and reporting obligations, with fines up to €7m or 1.4% of global turnover.
findings.remedy: Register and align security measures to Art. 21.
steps: Register with the competent authority
Baseline current measures against Art. 21 risk-management requirements

findings.title: NIS2 classification not yet determined
findings.detail: Operating without a confirmed NIS2 classification means obligations, registration deadlines and reporting duties may already be unmet.
findings.remedy: Run a formal scoping exercise against national transposition rules.
steps: Commission a NIS2 applicability assessment
Cross-check sector + size thresholds against Annexes I–II
Document the determination for the competent authority

questions.text: Under DORA, which type of financial entity are you?
questions.help: DORA applies to a broad set of financial entities and to the ICT providers serving them. The obligations scale with entity type and systemic importance.

findings.title: Full DORA ICT risk-management framework required
findings.detail: Credit institutions must operate a documented ICT risk-management framework, maintain a register of information on all ICT third-party arrangements, and manage concentration risk.
findings.remedy: Confirm the ICT risk framework and register of information are in place and current.
steps: Confirm board-approved ICT risk-management framework
Verify the register of information covers all ICT arrangements
Identify contracts supporting critical or important functions

options.label: Investment firm / asset manager / trading venue

findings.title: DORA third-party and resilience duties apply
findings.detail: Investment and asset-management firms must manage ICT third-party risk, test operational resilience and ensure critical functions can withstand disruption to cross-border ICT providers.
findings.remedy: Map critical/important functions to underlying ICT providers and their data locations.
steps: Inventory critical/important business functions
Map each to supporting ICT services and their processing locations
Assess exit and substitutability for each

findings.title: DORA applies to insurance undertakings
findings.detail: Insurers must embed ICT risk management and third-party oversight, including data-location transparency for outsourced functions.
findings.remedy: Extend existing outsourcing governance to meet DORA's ICT-specific requirements.
steps: Gap-assess current outsourcing policy against DORA Art. 28–30
Update contracts to include mandatory DORA clauses

findings.title: DORA ICT framework + PSD2 obligations
findings.detail: PIs and EMIs fall in DORA scope and simultaneously carry PSD2 obligations (SCA, AIS/PIS access, incident reporting to competent authority). ICT third-party risk, register of information and contractual clauses apply.
findings.remedy: Ensure the DORA framework is in place alongside PSD2 operational and outsourcing controls.
steps: Confirm DORA ICT risk framework covers PSD2 processes
Verify SCA and incident-reporting readiness
Register ICT third-party arrangements including data locations

findings.title: DORA applies to CASPs + MiCA authorisation
findings.detail: MiCA-authorised CASPs providing services in the EU are DORA-in-scope. ICT risk management, third-party arrangements and resilience testing apply alongside MiCA prudential and safeguarding rules.
findings.remedy: Align DORA ICT framework with MiCA authorisation and safeguarding requirements.
steps: Confirm DORA framework is fit for a MiCA-authorised firm
Cover crypto-custody arrangements as ICT third-party arrangements
Include CASP-specific scenarios in resilience testing

options.label: Other financial entity (crowdfunding, credit rating agency, benchmark administrator, etc.)

findings.title: DORA proportionality applies
findings.detail: Smaller or specialised financial entities benefit from a proportionate regime but core ICT risk and third-party obligations still apply.
findings.remedy: Confirm which proportionality carve-outs apply and document the rationale.
steps: Confirm entity type and any simplified regime
Document proportionality decisions

options.label: Not a financial entity under DORA

questions.text: For personal data, what is the primary jurisdiction of your data subjects?
questions.help: This determines whether EU GDPR, UK GDPR or both apply, and sets the baseline residency expectation.

findings.title: Dual EU/UK regime — divergence risk
findings.detail: Operating under both regimes means EU–UK data flows rely on the current UK adequacy decision, which is subject to periodic review and possible expiry.
findings.remedy: Maintain a fallback transfer mechanism (SCCs + IDTA) in case adequacy lapses.
steps: Confirm reliance on the EU→UK adequacy decision
Prepare SCC/IDTA fallback documentation

findings.title: Global footprint triggers transfer scrutiny
findings.detail: A global data-subject footprint substantially increases the surface area for unlawful cross-border transfers and jurisdictional conflict.
findings.remedy: Prioritise a full transfer-mapping exercise (Section D).
steps: Map all cross-border personal-data flows
Identify transfers lacking a valid Chapter V mechanism

questions.text: Has a data-flow map (data mapping / RoPA) been produced and kept current in the last 12 months?
questions.help: A Record of Processing Activities under GDPR Art. 30 — and an equivalent data-flow inventory — is the foundation of every residency control.

findings.title: Data mapping incomplete or stale
findings.detail: An out-of-date RoPA means residency findings in this report are working from partial visibility; new systems and flows may be unmapped.
findings.remedy: Refresh the RoPA and data-flow inventory before finalising architecture decisions.
steps: Refresh RoPA to cover all current systems
Reconcile against actual cloud/SaaS inventory
Establish a quarterly review cadence

findings.title: No record of processing activities
findings.detail: Absence of a RoPA is itself a GDPR compliance gap and prevents reliable residency assessment.
findings.remedy: Stand up a RoPA / data-flow inventory as a priority.
steps: Commission a data-discovery and mapping exercise
Document processing purposes, categories, recipients and locations
Assign ongoing ownership to the DPO / data office

questions.text: Which categories of sensitive data does your organisation process?
questions.help: Special-category and financial data carry heightened residency and security expectations across all regimes.

findings.title: Personal data in scope
findings.detail: General personal data must be processed with appropriate security and a lawful residency posture.
findings.remedy: Ensure all personal-data stores are covered by the residency controls in Sections C–D.
steps: Confirm all PII stores are inventoried
Apply baseline encryption and access control

findings.title: Special-category data present
findings.detail: Art. 9 data demands an explicit condition for processing plus enhanced safeguards; cross-border exposure is materially higher risk.
findings.remedy: Confirm an Art. 9 condition and lock storage to the highest-assurance region available.
steps: Document the Art. 9 processing condition for each dataset
Restrict special-category stores to EEA/UK regions
Apply enhanced encryption and least-privilege access

findings.title: Financial data supports critical or important functions
findings.detail: Financial and payment data typically supports critical or important functions under DORA — its residency and availability drive operational-resilience obligations, ICT third-party clauses and the register of information. National banking-secrecy rules and, for card data, PCI DSS impose additional obligations.
findings.remedy: Treat financial data stores as supporting critical or important functions; confirm PCI DSS scope for card data.
steps: Classify financial data stores by criticality
Confirm PCI DSS scope for cardholder data
Confirm resilience and residency for each store

findings.title: Behavioural data often flows to third parties
findings.detail: Analytics and behavioural datasets frequently transit to SaaS platforms in non-EEA jurisdictions, creating transfer exposure.
findings.remedy: Trace behavioural data to its downstream processors (Section E).
steps: Identify analytics/behavioural data recipients
Confirm processor agreements and processing locations

findings.title: Training data in scope of AI Act governance
findings.detail: Where AI systems are high-risk, training, validation and testing data are subject to specific governance and provenance requirements.
findings.remedy: Establish provenance and residency controls for training data (Section G).
steps: Inventory training/validation/test datasets
Document data provenance and lineage
Confirm residency of the training environment

findings.title: Business-critical data protection
findings.detail: Proprietary data loss can constitute a significant incident; NIS2 expects proportionate protection.
findings.remedy: Include proprietary data in the resilience and access-control scope.
steps: Classify proprietary data sensitivity
Apply access control consistent with NIS2 Art. 21

findings.title: Government/classified data demands sovereign controls
findings.detail: Restricted or classified data typically cannot lawfully reside on cloud services controlled from non-EU jurisdictions and may require High-assurance sovereign hosting.
findings.remedy: Confirm sovereign hosting and key custody for all classified data.
steps: Confirm national handling rules for the classification level
Restrict to sovereign / High-assurance platforms
Ensure keys are held under EU/national control

questions.text: Approximately what volume of sensitive data (personal, financial, special-category) do you hold?
questions.help: Volume scales both regulatory exposure and remediation effort. Breach impact and notification burden grow with volume.

findings.title: Material data volume raises breach impact
findings.detail: At multi-terabyte scale, a residency or security failure affects a large data-subject population, escalating notification and remediation cost.
findings.remedy: Prioritise encryption and access segmentation for the largest stores.
steps: Identify the largest sensitive-data stores
Confirm encryption and segmentation for each

findings.title: Large-scale processing
findings.detail: Large-scale processing of sensitive data triggers heightened accountability, likely a DPIA, and severe breach consequences.
findings.remedy: Confirm a DPIA is in place and residency is centrally governed.
steps: Confirm DPIA coverage for large-scale processing
Centralise residency governance

findings.title: Very large-scale processing
findings.detail: At this scale, systematic monitoring and DPIA obligations are almost certainly engaged and any residency failure is systemically material.
findings.remedy: Treat residency as a board-level operational risk.
steps: Elevate data residency to the enterprise risk register
Ensure DPIA and prior-consultation readiness

questions.text: Which cloud and hosting platforms run your production systems?
questions.help: Operator jurisdiction and region selection are the primary levers of data residency.

findings.title: Production workloads in non-EU cloud regions
findings.detail: Personal data processed in non-EU regions constitutes a restricted transfer requiring a valid Chapter V mechanism and, for US operators, exposure to foreign government access.
findings.remedy: Confirm which workloads sit outside the EU and lock personal-data workloads to EU regions.
steps: Enumerate all non-EU regions in use
Identify personal-data workloads among them
Migrate or region-lock personal-data workloads to EU

findings.title: Azure workloads in non-EU regions
findings.detail: Non-EU Azure regions processing personal data create restricted transfers and potential CLOUD Act exposure via a US-controlled operator.
findings.remedy: Region-lock personal-data workloads to EU Azure regions.
steps: Audit Azure region configuration
Apply Azure Policy to restrict region deployment
Migrate non-compliant workloads

findings.title: GCP workloads in non-EU regions
findings.detail: Non-EU GCP regions processing personal data create restricted transfers and potential CLOUD Act exposure via a US-controlled operator.
findings.remedy: Region-lock personal-data workloads to EU GCP regions.
steps: Audit GCP region configuration
Apply Organization Policy to restrict region deployment
Migrate non-compliant workloads

findings.title: US-HQ operator in use (Oracle Cloud) — even EU-only
findings.detail: Oracle Cloud EU regions constrain data location, but operator jurisdiction remains the United States; extraterritorial access risk under the CLOUD Act should still be assessed at the workload level.
findings.remedy: Assess CLOUD Act residual risk for the most sensitive workloads.
steps: Confirm all Oracle Cloud regions are EU
Assess residual CLOUD Act exposure for the most sensitive workloads
Consider EU-controlled alternatives for highest tier

findings.title: Oracle Cloud workloads in non-EU regions
findings.detail: Non-EU Oracle Cloud regions processing personal data create restricted transfers and CLOUD Act exposure via a US-controlled operator.
findings.remedy: Region-lock personal-data workloads to EU Oracle Cloud regions.
steps: Audit Oracle Cloud region configuration
Restrict provisioning to EU regions
Migrate non-compliant workloads

findings.title: US-HQ operator in use (IBM Cloud) — even EU-only
findings.detail: IBM Cloud EU regions constrain data location, but operator jurisdiction remains the United States; assess residual extraterritorial access risk.
findings.remedy: Confirm region residency and assess CLOUD Act residual risk.
steps: Confirm all IBM Cloud regions are EU
Assess residual CLOUD Act exposure for the most sensitive workloads

findings.title: IBM Cloud workloads in non-EU regions
findings.detail: Non-EU IBM Cloud regions processing personal data create restricted transfers and CLOUD Act exposure via a US-controlled operator.
findings.remedy: Region-lock personal-data workloads to EU IBM Cloud regions.
steps: Audit IBM Cloud region configuration
Restrict provisioning to EU regions
Migrate non-compliant workloads

findings.title: Salesforce / Heroku is a US-HQ SaaS operator
findings.detail: Salesforce and Heroku operate under US jurisdiction; even EU-hosted tenants remain within CLOUD Act reach via the operator. Assess supplementary measures and data residency clauses.
findings.remedy: Confirm EU hosting, tenant isolation and DPF certification (if applicable).
steps: Confirm EU data residency for the Salesforce org
Check Salesforce DPF-list entry
Add supplementary encryption for sensitive fields

findings.title: Snowflake — US-HQ operator, region matters
findings.detail: Snowflake supports EU regions but is a US-HQ operator; region selection alone does not remove CLOUD Act exposure.
findings.remedy: Confirm EU region + assess CLOUD Act residual risk.
steps: Confirm Snowflake account region is EU
Enable customer-managed encryption keys where available
Assess DPF certification and supplementary measures

findings.title: Databricks — US-HQ operator, region matters
findings.detail: Databricks supports EU regions but is a US-HQ operator; region selection alone does not remove CLOUD Act exposure — relevant especially for training-data workloads.
findings.remedy: Confirm EU region and assess CLOUD Act residual risk; consider EU-controlled ML platforms for the most sensitive workloads.
steps: Confirm Databricks workspace region is EU
Assess CLOUD Act residual risk
Evaluate sovereign alternatives for the most sensitive workloads

options.label: Sovereign / EU-controlled cloud (e.g. EUCS-aligned, Gaia-X, national)

findings.title: Sovereign platform in use
findings.detail: An EU-controlled or sovereign platform substantially reduces jurisdictional exposure for regulated workloads.
findings.remedy: Confirm the assurance level meets the sensitivity of hosted data.
steps: Verify certified assurance level
Match assurance level to data classification

findings.title: Managed-hosting supply-chain dependency
findings.detail: Colocation and managed hosting introduce a supply-chain dependency that must be governed under NIS2 supply-chain security.
findings.remedy: Include hosting provider in supply-chain risk assessment.
steps: Add hosting provider to the supplier register
Confirm physical and jurisdictional controls

questions.text: For each sensitive data category, where is it stored and processed today?
questions.help: This is the residency heart of the assessment. 'Unknown' is scored as a risk in its own right.

us-cloud.title: {row} located in a non-EU jurisdiction
us-cloud.detail: Storing {rowlower} in US/non-EU cloud is a restricted transfer that is unlawful absent a valid mechanism, and exposes the data to foreign government access requests.
us-cloud.remedy: Migrate {rowlower} to an EU region or a valid transfer mechanism with supplementary measures.
steps: Confirm the exact location and operator of {rowlower}
Assess whether a valid Chapter V mechanism exists
Migrate to EU region or implement SCCs + supplementary measures

multi.title: {row} replicated across multiple regions
multi.detail: Multi-region replication of {rowlower} means copies exist in non-EU jurisdictions, each an independent transfer that must be justified.
multi.remedy: Constrain replication topology so {rowlower} never leaves approved regions.
steps: Map the replication topology for {rowlower}
Reconfigure replication to EU-approved regions only

unknown.title: Location of {row} is unknown
unknown.detail: You cannot demonstrate compliance for data whose location you cannot state. This is a visibility gap that must be closed first.
steps: Run automated data discovery for {rowlower}
Record findings in the RoPA

us-dpf.title: {row} transferred to a DPF-certified US processor
us-dpf.detail: Transfers of {rowlower} to US recipients certified under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework benefit from adequacy. Schrems-III risk remains open — reconfirm certification periodically.
us-dpf.remedy: Verify DPF certification and maintain SCC + TIA fallback for {rowlower}.
steps: Verify recipient on commerce.gov Data Privacy Framework Program list
Document DPF reliance in the RoPA
Maintain SCC fallback

eu-backup.title: {row} backed up outside the EU
eu-backup.detail: Encrypted non-EU backup of {rowlower} is lower risk but the encrypted copy is still a transfer; key custody determines whether it is defensible.
eu-backup.remedy: Confirm backup encryption keys are held under EU control.
steps: Confirm backup encryption standard
Confirm keys are EU-held and not accessible to the non-EU operator

questions.text: Are data-residency constraints enforced technically (e.g. region-lock policy) or only by convention?
questions.help: Policy-as-code prevents residency drift; convention alone tends to erode as teams deploy new services.

findings.title: Partial residency enforcement
findings.detail: Where residency is only partly enforced, new or shadow deployments can silently place data in non-approved regions.
findings.remedy: Extend region-lock guardrails across all accounts and subscriptions.
steps: Apply region-restriction policy to all cloud accounts
Add residency checks to CI/CD deployment gates

findings.title: No technical residency enforcement
findings.detail: Data-protection-by-design (Art. 25) expects technical enforcement; convention-only controls routinely fail as the estate grows.
findings.remedy: Implement organisation-wide region-restriction guardrails.
steps: Define approved regions per data classification
Deploy preventative guardrails (e.g. SCPs / Azure Policy)
Alert on any attempted non-compliant deployment

questions.text: Do personal data flows leave the EEA (or the UK, for UK data)?
questions.help: Any egress of personal data to a third country is a 'restricted transfer' requiring a Chapter V safeguard.

options.label: No — personal data stays within EEA/UK
Yes, but only to adequate countries

findings.title: Transfers rely on adequacy decisions
findings.detail: Adequacy decisions are periodically reviewed and can be suspended; reliance on adequacy alone carries residual risk.
findings.remedy: Maintain a fallback safeguard in case an adequacy decision lapses.
steps: List destination countries and their adequacy status
Prepare SCC fallback for each

options.label: Yes, under SCCs / IDTA with safeguards

findings.title: Transfers rely on SCCs — verify supplementary measures
findings.detail: Post-Schrems II, SCCs alone are insufficient; a transfer impact assessment and supplementary measures are required, especially for US transfers.
findings.remedy: Confirm a TIA and supplementary technical measures exist for each SCC transfer.
steps: Confirm SCCs are the current (2021) modules
Complete a transfer impact assessment per destination
Implement supplementary measures (e.g. encryption with EU-held keys)

options.label: Yes — to US recipients certified under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework (DPF)

findings.title: Transfers relying on EU-US DPF adequacy
findings.detail: US recipients certified under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework (Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2023/1795, 10 July 2023) benefit from adequacy. Reconfirm the recipient DPF certification periodically — a future CJEU challenge remains possible; UK-established firms can additionally rely on the UK-US Data Bridge extension (October 2023).
findings.remedy: Maintain the DPF certification check and a fallback (SCCs + TIA) in case adequacy lapses.
steps: Verify each US recipient on the DPF Program list at commerce.gov
Document reliance on DPF adequacy in your RoPA
Prepare SCC + TIA fallback documentation

options.label: Yes, without a documented mechanism / unsure

findings.title: Undocumented international transfers
findings.detail: Transferring personal data abroad without a valid, documented Chapter V mechanism is a direct GDPR breach exposing the organisation to the top tier of fines.
findings.remedy: Halt or lawfully paper every undocumented transfer as a priority.
steps: Identify every cross-border personal-data flow
Implement SCCs/IDTA + TIA for each, or repatriate
Document all mechanisms in the RoPA

questions.text: Have transfer impact assessments (TIAs) been completed for transfers to non-adequate countries?
questions.help: Schrems II requires a case-by-case assessment of whether the destination's laws undermine the SCCs, plus supplementary measures where they do.

findings.title: Incomplete transfer impact assessments
findings.detail: Gaps in TIA coverage leave some transfers unassessed and potentially unlawful.
findings.remedy: Complete TIAs for all remaining non-adequate transfers.
steps: List transfers lacking a TIA
Complete and document each TIA

findings.title: No transfer impact assessments
findings.detail: Without TIAs, reliance on SCCs is not defensible following Schrems II.
findings.remedy: Run TIAs for all restricted transfers and add supplementary measures.
steps: Build a TIA template aligned to EDPB recommendations
Assess each destination's surveillance regime
Apply supplementary measures where risk is identified

questions.text: Do you rely on any cloud or data-processing service that would be subject to EU Data Act switching / portability obligations?
questions.help: The Data Act (Regulation (EU) 2023/2854) applies from 12 September 2025; cloud switching provisions phase in later. Providers and their customers both have roles.

options.label: Yes — as a customer of cloud / data-processing services

findings.title: Data Act switching rights available
findings.detail: As a customer, the Data Act grants you rights to switch and port data between providers on transparent terms; ensure your contracts reflect these rights.
findings.remedy: Review provider contracts for Data Act switching / portability terms.
steps: Confirm contract includes Data Act switching provisions
Verify functional-equivalence obligations
Track upcoming Data Act commencement milestones

options.label: Yes — as a provider of cloud / data-processing services

findings.title: Data Act provider obligations apply
findings.detail: As a provider, you must facilitate customer switching, ensure portability of exportable data, meet contractual-fairness rules, and safeguard against unlawful third-country access to non-personal data held in the EU.
findings.remedy: Build a Data Act compliance programme covering switching, portability and non-personal-data access safeguards.
steps: Document switching / portability procedures
Update customer contracts for Data Act terms
Implement safeguards against unlawful third-country access to non-personal data

options.label: Not applicable / EU Data Act not in scope

questions.text: Do you maintain Data Processing Agreements (GDPR Art. 28) with all processors?
questions.help: Every processor handling personal data on your behalf must be bound by Art. 28 terms, including subprocessor and location controls.

findings.title: Processor agreements incomplete
findings.detail: Any processor without a compliant DPA processes personal data without a lawful basis for that processing relationship.
findings.remedy: Close DPA gaps and confirm location/subprocessor clauses.
steps: Reconcile the processor list against signed DPAs
Execute compliant DPAs for gaps
Confirm each DPA specifies processing locations

findings.title: Widespread processor-agreement gaps
findings.detail: Relying on DPAs only for major vendors leaves a long tail of SaaS and analytics processors unbound and unmonitored.
findings.remedy: Undertake a full processor discovery and remediation.
steps: Discover all processors (including SaaS/analytics)
Prioritise by data sensitivity
Execute DPAs across the estate

findings.title: No processor agreements in place
findings.detail: Processing personal data through processors without Art. 28 agreements is a systemic GDPR breach.
findings.remedy: Treat as an immediate remediation programme.
steps: Stand up a processor-governance workstream
Inventory and rank all processors
Execute DPAs, prioritising sensitive-data processors

questions.text: Do you maintain a register of ICT third-party arrangements (DORA register of information)?
questions.help: DORA requires financial entities to maintain a structured register of all ICT third-party service arrangements, flagging those supporting critical or important functions.

findings.title: DORA register of information incomplete
findings.detail: An incomplete register means concentration and substitutability risk cannot be assessed and supervisory reporting will fail.
findings.remedy: Complete the register to the RTS template.
steps: Populate the register to the regulatory template
Flag arrangements supporting critical/important functions
Establish maintenance ownership

findings.title: No DORA register of information
findings.detail: Absence of the register is a direct DORA gap and blocks any assessment of ICT concentration risk, including data-location concentration.
findings.remedy: Build the register as a foundational DORA deliverable.
steps: Adopt the regulatory register template
Inventory all ICT arrangements and their data locations
Identify concentration on single providers/regions

questions.text: Do you have visibility of where your key SaaS and ICT providers actually process and store your data?
questions.help: Data-location transparency is required under both GDPR (Art. 28) and DORA (Art. 30); default vendor configurations often place data outside the EU.

options.label: Full visibility — locations documented per provider

findings.title: Partial vendor data-location visibility
findings.detail: Where vendor processing locations are unclear, undisclosed non-EU processing and subprocessor chains may exist.
findings.remedy: Require location disclosure from every material provider.
steps: Request data-location and subprocessor disclosure from providers
Update the register/RoPA with confirmed locations

findings.title: No vendor data-location visibility
findings.detail: Without knowing where providers process your data, residency compliance cannot be asserted and DORA contractual requirements are unmet.
findings.remedy: Establish data-location transparency contractually and technically.
steps: Add mandatory data-location clauses to contracts
Obtain current subprocessor lists
Verify against actual traffic/region telemetry where possible

questions.text: Are subprocessor changes controlled (prior notice + right to object)?
questions.help: Uncontrolled subprocessor chains are a common route by which data silently moves to new jurisdictions.

options.label: Yes — notice and objection rights in place

findings.title: Uncontrolled subprocessor changes
findings.detail: Without prior-notice and objection rights, a processor can add a subprocessor in a new jurisdiction without your knowledge, moving data across borders.
findings.remedy: Insert subprocessor-control clauses and monitor subprocessor lists.
steps: Add prior-notice + objection clauses to DPAs
Subscribe to provider subprocessor-change notifications
Review subprocessor lists quarterly

questions.text: Where are production backups physically stored?
questions.help: Backups are frequently the forgotten residency exposure — a compliant primary with a non-EU backup is still non-compliant.

findings.title: Encrypted backup held outside the EU
findings.detail: An encrypted non-EU backup is a transfer; defensibility hinges on key custody remaining under EU control.
findings.remedy: Confirm EU key custody or repatriate the secondary copy.
steps: Confirm backup encryption keys are EU-held
Confirm the operator cannot access plaintext

findings.title: US backup relying on DPF adequacy
findings.detail: Backups stored with a DPF-certified US recipient rely on adequacy; the backup is still a transfer and DPF certification must be maintained and reconfirmed periodically.
findings.remedy: Verify and monitor the backup provider DPF certification status.
steps: Verify the backup provider on commerce.gov Data Privacy Framework Program list
Document reliance in the RoPA
Maintain SCC fallback in case adequacy lapses

findings.title: Backups stored in a non-EU jurisdiction
findings.detail: Non-EU backups replicate every residency and transfer exposure of the primary, often silently and at full data volume. Without DPF adequacy or another Chapter V mechanism, this is a direct GDPR breach.
findings.remedy: Region-lock backups to the EU as an immediate action, or move to a DPF-certified provider.
steps: Reconfigure backup targets to EU regions
Purge or migrate existing non-EU backup copies
Verify retention/deletion of migrated copies

findings.title: Backup location unknown
findings.detail: Unknown backup location is a visibility gap that frequently conceals the largest residency exposure in the estate.
findings.remedy: Determine backup topology before other remediation.
steps: Map the full backup and replication topology
Document all backup destinations

questions.text: Is data encrypted at rest, and who controls the encryption keys?
questions.help: Encryption with customer-held (EU-custodied) keys is a recognised supplementary measure for transfers and a strong residency safeguard.

options.label: Yes — AES-256 with EU-held customer-managed keys
Yes — but keys managed by the (non-EU) provider

findings.title: Encryption keys held by non-EU provider
findings.detail: Provider-managed keys mean the operator (and its home jurisdiction) can technically access plaintext, weakening encryption as a transfer safeguard.
findings.remedy: Move to customer-managed keys held under EU control (e.g. external key store / HYOK).
steps: Adopt customer-managed keys (CMK/BYOK)
Host key material in an EU-controlled KMS/HSM
Consider Hold-Your-Own-Key for the most sensitive data

findings.title: Inadequate encryption at rest
findings.detail: Weak or partial encryption fails Art. 32 'appropriate measures' and cannot serve as a transfer supplementary measure.
findings.remedy: Standardise strong encryption at rest across sensitive stores.
steps: Adopt AES-256 (or equivalent) for all sensitive stores
Remediate unencrypted stores first

findings.title: Sensitive data unencrypted at rest
findings.detail: Unencrypted sensitive data at rest is a serious security-of-processing failure and dramatically increases breach severity.
findings.remedy: Encrypt all sensitive data at rest immediately.
steps: Enable encryption at rest on all sensitive stores
Prioritise special-category and financial data
Verify no plaintext backups remain

questions.text: Is data encrypted in transit (TLS) for all connections to and between cloud systems?
questions.help: In-transit encryption is table stakes for Art. 32 and prevents interception during cross-border transit.

findings.title: Gaps in in-transit encryption
findings.detail: Unencrypted internal or inter-service traffic is exploitable and undermines the security-of-processing baseline.
findings.remedy: Enforce TLS on all links, including east-west traffic.
steps: Enforce TLS 1.2+ on all connections
Enable mutual TLS for service-to-service traffic

findings.title: In-transit encryption not assured
findings.detail: Without enforced transport encryption, data crossing networks (and borders) is exposed to interception.
findings.remedy: Mandate transport encryption as a baseline control.
steps: Mandate TLS across all ingress/egress
Disable plaintext protocols

questions.text: For financial entities: have you tested that critical functions survive disruption to a cross-border ICT provider?
questions.help: DORA requires digital operational resilience testing, including scenarios where a key ICT/cloud provider or region becomes unavailable.

findings.title: Resilience testing not yet performed
findings.detail: Untested resilience means concentration on a single cross-border provider or region may be an unquantified single point of failure.
findings.remedy: Schedule resilience testing including provider-loss scenarios.
steps: Define severe-but-plausible ICT disruption scenarios
Test failover and provider substitution
Document results and remediation

findings.title: No operational resilience testing
findings.detail: Absence of resilience testing is a DORA gap and leaves cross-border concentration risk unmanaged.
findings.remedy: Establish a digital operational resilience testing programme.
steps: Stand up a DORA testing programme
Prioritise critical-function and single-provider scenarios
Feed results into the ICT risk framework

questions.text: For UK-regulated financial firms: are impact tolerances set for important business services (UK Operational Resilience)?
questions.help: FCA PS21/3 and PRA SS2/21 require identification of important business services, impact tolerances, mapping and scenario testing. Since March 2025, firms must be able to remain within tolerances for severe-but-plausible scenarios.

options.label: Yes — impact tolerances set, mapping and testing complete
Partial — tolerances set but mapping / testing incomplete

findings.title: UK Op Res mapping / testing incomplete
findings.detail: Impact tolerances without complete mapping and scenario testing cannot be shown to be defensible against a severe-but-plausible disruption. Post-March 2025 supervisory expectations require evidence.
findings.remedy: Complete mapping of important business services and scenario testing.
steps: Complete mapping to underlying resources incl. ICT and data locations
Run severe-but-plausible scenario tests
Update the self-assessment document

findings.title: UK operational-resilience framework not established
findings.detail: Post-March 2025, the FCA and PRA expect firms to be able to demonstrate they can remain within impact tolerances for important business services. Absence is a material gap.
findings.remedy: Stand up the UK Op Res framework as a priority.
steps: Identify important business services
Set impact tolerances
Map underlying resources
Design and run scenario tests
Produce the self-assessment

questions.text: Do you develop, deploy or fine-tune AI/ML systems on personal or sensitive data?
questions.help: AI processing frequently defaults to non-EU compute regions and raises training-data governance obligations.

options.label: No AI/ML on personal or sensitive data

findings.title: AI data-governance baseline applies
findings.detail: Even non-high-risk AI benefits from documented data provenance and residency to avoid future re-work as scope tightens.
findings.remedy: Establish baseline AI data-governance and training-data residency.
steps: Document training-data sources and residency
Set a policy for AI compute region selection

options.label: Yes — high-risk AI (e.g. credit scoring, life/health insurance pricing, employment/HR AI, biometric identification)

findings.title: High-risk AI data-governance obligations
findings.detail: Annex III of the AI Act enumerates high-risk categories including biometric identification (item 1), employment/workforce management (item 4), creditworthiness (item 5(b)), and life/health insurance risk-and-pricing (item 5(c)). High-risk AI must meet Art. 10 data-governance requirements — relevant, representative, error-checked datasets with documented provenance — plus record-keeping and human oversight.
findings.remedy: Implement AI Act data-governance controls and confirm training residency.
steps: Classify AI systems against Annex III high-risk categories
Implement data-governance and provenance controls (Art. 10)
Confirm training/validation environments reside in approved regions
Establish record-keeping and human-oversight measures

questions.text: Where does AI model training and inference compute physically run?
questions.help: Training compute frequently defaults to US regions (e.g. managed ML platforms), moving sensitive training data across borders.

findings.title: AI compute partly outside the EU
findings.detail: Non-EU training or inference moves sensitive training data across borders — a transfer that often escapes the RoPA entirely.
findings.remedy: Region-lock AI compute for sensitive workloads to the EU.
steps: Audit ML platform default regions
Region-lock training and inference for sensitive data
Update the RoPA to capture AI data flows

options.label: Primarily US / non-EU compute, with DPF-certified provider

findings.title: AI compute at DPF-certified US provider
findings.detail: Running training/inference on sensitive data at a DPF-certified US recipient benefits from adequacy; residual Schrems-III risk plus DORA and AI Act residency and record-keeping obligations still apply.
findings.remedy: Verify DPF certification and add AI-specific contractual controls; consider sovereign alternatives for the most sensitive workloads.
steps: Verify the AI compute provider on commerce.gov Data Privacy Framework Program list
Add AI-specific data-protection and data-provenance terms
Consider EU sovereign AI compute for the most sensitive workloads

findings.title: AI compute located outside the EU
findings.detail: Running training/inference on sensitive data in non-EU regions without a valid Chapter V mechanism is a restricted transfer at scale, frequently undocumented, and may breach DORA and the AI Act simultaneously.
findings.remedy: Repatriate sensitive AI compute to the EU or an approved sovereign platform, or move to a DPF-certified provider.
steps: Identify all non-EU AI compute touching sensitive data
Migrate to EU / sovereign ML platforms
Implement provenance tracking for training data

findings.title: AI compute location unknown
findings.detail: Unknown AI compute location is a common blind spot where the largest undocumented transfers occur.
findings.remedy: Determine where AI workloads actually execute.
steps: Trace AI platform region configuration
Document AI data flows in the RoPA

questions.text: Do you use, embed or provide any general-purpose AI (GPAI) model in production (e.g. LLMs, foundation models)?
questions.help: GPAI obligations under EU AI Act Chapter V (Arts. 51–56) attach differently depending on your role — provider, downstream user, or integrator.

options.label: No — we do not use GPAI
Yes — we deploy third-party GPAI (downstream user)

findings.title: GPAI downstream-user obligations
findings.detail: Downstream users of GPAI benefit from the transparency documentation provided by the GPAI provider, must respect copyright policy, and must ensure their use case does not silently turn a general model into an Annex III high-risk system without corresponding controls.
findings.remedy: Integrate GPAI provider transparency documentation into your AI governance.
steps: Obtain and archive GPAI provider transparency documentation
Ensure your use case does not create an unclassified high-risk system
Track EU AI Office guidance updates

options.label: Yes — we develop / provide our own GPAI models placed on the EU market

findings.title: GPAI provider obligations apply
findings.detail: Providers of GPAI models placed on the EU market are subject to Chapter V: technical documentation, transparency to downstream deployers, EU copyright compliance policy, publication of a training-data summary, cooperation with the AI Office. Systemic-risk GPAI (compute threshold under Art. 51(2)) owes additional model-evaluation, adversarial-testing and incident-reporting duties. GPAI provisions apply from 2 August 2025.
findings.remedy: Stand up a GPAI compliance programme covering documentation, transparency, copyright and cooperation.
steps: Produce technical documentation per AI Office template
Publish training-data summary
Adopt an EU copyright compliance policy
If systemic-risk: model evaluation, adversarial testing, cybersecurity, incident reporting

options.label: Yes — we embed third-party GPAI into products or services we sell

findings.title: Integrator may become provider under Art. 25
findings.detail: Firms placing an AI system on the market under their own name may be treated as providers of the resulting system (Art. 25 — provider substitution). Assess whether provider-level obligations attach to the integrated system in addition to base-model provider obligations.
findings.remedy: Assess Art. 25 provider-substitution risk for each integrated GPAI product.
steps: Map each product embedding third-party GPAI
Determine if you place the system under your own name
Adopt provider-level obligations where applicable

questions.text: For UK-established firms using AI/ML: how aligned is your AI governance with UK principles-based expectations (ICO / FCA / PRA)?
questions.help: The UK follows a principles-based, regulator-led AI approach. ICO guidance on AI and data protection, FCA supervisory expectations for AI in regulated activities, and PRA/BoE SS1/23 on model risk management for AI/ML apply.

refs.a: ICO AI guidance; FCA AI update; PRA/BoE SS1/23

options.label: Yes — governance evidenced against ICO / FCA / PRA principles
Partial — awareness of ICO / FCA / PRA expectations, evidence incomplete

findings.title: UK AI governance evidence incomplete
findings.detail: Principles-based expectations still require evidence — DPIAs for AI processing (ICO), consumer-duty and senior-manager accountability (FCA), and model risk governance (PRA/BoE SS1/23). Partial alignment is a common finding; document controls end-to-end.
findings.remedy: Close the evidence gaps against each supervisor guideline.
steps: Complete DPIAs for AI processing personal data (ICO)
Document FCA-relevant AI governance for regulated activities
Adopt SS1/23 model risk management framework for material AI/ML

options.label: No — UK AI governance not established

findings.title: UK AI governance not established
findings.detail: Absence of AI governance in a UK-regulated firm exposes the firm to ICO enforcement on data-protection aspects and to FCA/PRA supervisory action for regulated activities. PRA/BoE SS1/23 is now the reference framework for banks and insurers on AI/ML model risk.
findings.remedy: Stand up an AI governance framework aligned to the three UK supervisory streams.
steps: Establish an AI governance forum with named executive owner
Complete DPIAs for AI processing (ICO)
Adopt SS1/23 model risk management principles
Align to FCA senior-manager accountability and consumer duty

options.label: Not applicable (no UK establishment or no AI use)

questions.text: What is the jurisdiction of the entity that ultimately controls your primary cloud platform?
questions.help: Operator jurisdiction — not just data-centre location — determines exposure to extraterritorial access laws (e.g. US CLOUD Act).

findings.title: US operator with sovereign boundary
findings.detail: Sovereign-boundary offerings from US operators reduce but do not eliminate jurisdictional exposure; the degree of protection depends on operational control and key custody.
findings.remedy: Validate the sovereign offering's operational-control and key-custody claims against your data classification.
steps: Review the sovereign offering's control model
Confirm EU-personnel operation and EU key custody
Assess residual CLOUD Act exposure

findings.title: US-controlled cloud for regulated data
findings.detail: A US-controlled operator is subject to US extraterritorial access laws regardless of data-centre location, a recognised Schrems II concern.
findings.remedy: For the most sensitive workloads, evaluate sovereign or EU-controlled alternatives.
steps: Classify workloads by sensitivity
Evaluate sovereign options for the highest tier
Apply supplementary measures (EU-held keys) in the interim

findings.title: Non-EU operator jurisdiction
findings.detail: Any non-EU operator jurisdiction should be assessed for extraterritorial access risk and adequacy.
findings.remedy: Assess the jurisdiction's access laws and adequacy status.
steps: Assess the operator jurisdiction's surveillance regime
Confirm a valid transfer mechanism

questions.text: For regulated workloads, is the cloud service certified to an assurance level (e.g. EUCS Substantial/High)?
questions.help: Assurance certification provides objective evidence of the controls appropriate to the sensitivity of hosted data.

findings.title: Substantial assurance in place
findings.detail: Substantial assurance suits many workloads; the most sensitive or sovereignty-critical data may warrant High.
findings.remedy: Confirm the assurance level matches your highest data classification.
steps: Map workloads to required assurance levels
Escalate the most sensitive workloads to High where needed

findings.title: Basic assurance may under-serve regulated workloads
findings.detail: EUCS Basic covers low-sensitivity workloads. Regulated data — especially personal, financial, or special-category — typically requires Substantial or High assurance for defensibility.
findings.remedy: Match assurance level to workload sensitivity; escalate regulated workloads above Basic.
steps: Identify workloads currently on Basic-assured platforms
Reclassify per data sensitivity
Migrate or contract for Substantial or High assurance where needed

findings.title: No cloud assurance certification
findings.detail: Without a recognised assurance level, the appropriateness of cloud security controls for regulated data cannot be objectively demonstrated.
findings.remedy: Pursue assurance certification for platforms hosting regulated data.
steps: Identify platforms hosting regulated data
Target an appropriate assurance level
Include assurance in future procurement criteria

questions.text: For any 'sovereign-boundary' or EU-controlled cloud offering, which controls are contractually and operationally in place?
questions.help: An offering marketed as 'sovereign' but without contractual, operational and cryptographic controls is not sovereign in a legal sense. This question fires the evidence side of Q_H1.

options.label: EU-only operations personnel (customer support and platform operators are EU nationals)
Contractual protection against extraterritorial disclosure requests (e.g. CLOUD Act, FISA §702)
Sub-processor list restricted to EU-jurisdiction entities
Local operating entity with EU jurisdiction of dispute resolution
None of the above / not documented

findings.title: Sovereign offering claimed without documented controls
findings.detail: An offering marketed as 'sovereign' but without documented EU-personnel operations, customer-held keys, anti-disclosure clauses or sub-processor limits is not sovereign in a legal sense — CLOUD Act and other extraterritorial exposures remain.
findings.remedy: Document each sovereignty control contractually or select a genuinely sovereign platform.
steps: Request contractual evidence for each sovereignty claim
Verify EU-personnel operations model
Confirm key custody arrangements
Restrict sub-processor list to EU jurisdictions

questions.text: Do your cloud/ICT contracts grant audit and inspection rights over data handling?
questions.help: Audit rights are explicitly required under DORA (Art. 30) and expected under NIS2 supply-chain security and GDPR Art. 28.

options.label: Yes — full audit and inspection rights

findings.title: Limited audit rights
findings.detail: Report-only rights may not satisfy DORA's requirement for effective audit and access, including for critical/important functions.
findings.remedy: Negotiate fuller audit and access rights for critical arrangements.
steps: Identify contracts supporting critical/important functions
Negotiate on-site/access and audit rights
Document supervisory access provisions

findings.title: No contractual audit rights
findings.detail: Absence of audit rights breaches DORA contractual requirements and prevents verification of data-location and security claims.
findings.remedy: Insert mandatory DORA audit and access clauses.
steps: Add DORA-mandated clauses to ICT contracts
Prioritise critical-function providers
Confirm regulator access rights

questions.text: Who owns data-residency decisions in your organisation?
questions.help: NIS2 places accountability on management bodies; unclear ownership is a common root cause of residency drift.

options.label: Clear executive owner with a governance forum
Shared across teams, no single owner

findings.title: Diffuse residency ownership
findings.detail: Without a single accountable owner, residency decisions are made inconsistently at team level and drift over time.
findings.remedy: Assign an accountable executive and a governance forum.
steps: Assign an accountable executive for data residency
Establish a cross-functional governance forum
Define decision rights and escalation

findings.title: No accountable owner for residency
findings.detail: NIS2 requires management-body accountability for cyber risk; unowned residency risk cannot be governed and exposes management personally.
findings.remedy: Establish accountable ownership at management-body level.
steps: Nominate a management-body owner
Brief the board on NIS2 accountability
Stand up governance and reporting

questions.text: For UK-regulated financial firms: do you rely on providers that may be designated Critical Third Parties (CTPs) under FSMA 2023?
questions.help: HM Treasury (on recommendation of FCA / PRA / BoE) designates CTPs. Designated CTPs are subject to six Fundamental Rules and joint FCA / PRA / BoE oversight. The rules bind the provider, but your own resilience accountability is undiminished.

refs.a: FSMA 2023 Part 9; FCA PS24/16; PRA PS16/24

options.label: Yes — we rely on likely / designated CTPs and understand our own residual duties

findings.title: CTP dependency identified and managed
findings.detail: CTP designations bind the provider under FCA / PRA / BoE oversight, but your own outsourcing, resilience and exit-planning duties are undiminished. Maintain governance directly.
findings.remedy: Maintain outsourcing governance and exit-plan readiness for CTP arrangements.
steps: Identify all critical arrangements with likely CTPs
Confirm outsourcing controls remain in place
Update exit plans and concentration-risk analysis

options.label: Unsure — CTP status of key providers not established

findings.title: CTP dependency status unclear
findings.detail: Not knowing which of your providers is (or may be) a designated CTP prevents effective concentration-risk and exit-plan design.
findings.remedy: Establish which providers are likely CTPs and plan accordingly.
steps: List providers supporting important business services
Assess likelihood of CTP designation via HM Treasury
Refresh concentration-risk analysis

questions.text: Can you detect and report a personal-data breach within 72 hours (GDPR) and a major incident within NIS2/DORA windows?
questions.help: GDPR requires notification within 72 hours; NIS2 requires an early warning within 24 hours and a full report within 72; DORA (via Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/301) requires initial notification within 4 hours of classifying an incident as major, an intermediate report within 72 hours, and a final report within 1 month.

refs.a: Art. 19; Comm. Del. Reg. (EU) 2025/301 (initial 4h / intermediate 72h / final 1 month)

options.label: Yes — tested detection and reporting process
Process exists but untested / unclear on cross-border

findings.title: Incident reporting readiness unproven
findings.detail: Overlapping GDPR/NIS2/DORA windows are hard to meet without a tested process, especially where data spans multiple jurisdictions and authorities.
findings.remedy: Test the incident-reporting process against all applicable regimes.
steps: Map notification duties across GDPR/NIS2/DORA
Run a cross-border breach tabletop
Pre-identify each competent authority and template

findings.title: Incident reporting not assured
findings.detail: Missing statutory reporting windows compounds an incident with regulatory penalties across multiple regimes.
findings.remedy: Establish a multi-regime incident detection and reporting capability.
steps: Stand up incident detection and triage
Build a multi-regime notification playbook
Establish 24/72-hour reporting readiness

questions.text: What is your compliance tolerance for this assessment?
questions.help: Shapes how aggressively the roadmap sequences remediation.

options.label: Minimal — acceptable with a short-term plan
Moderate — acceptable if residual risk is low

questions.text: What is your investment appetite for remediation across Phases 1–3?
questions.help: Used to frame the roadmap's ambition and sequencing.

options.label: Low — quick wins only for now

questions.text: Which outcomes matter most for the target architecture?
questions.help: Frames the strategic narrative in the report's roadmap.

options.label: Data sovereignty as a market differentiator
